c1.story:
It is a May evening in Delhi, the thermometer refuses to drop, and every air conditioner in the city is running. The electricity cooling your room could have come from an NTPC coal plant in Singrauli, a hydro station on a Himalayan river, a private coal plant on the Gujarat coast selling on the power exchange that very hour, or, until sunset, a solar park in the Rajasthan desert. Four very different ways of making the same unit, and four very different ways of getting paid for it.

The first door is the regulated utility: NTPC, NHPC, SJVN, NLC India. The regulator lets it earn a fixed return on every rupee of equity it invests in a plant, with fuel costs passed through to the buyer. Its profit grows in one way only, by building more plants. Heatwave or cool summer, the return is broadly the same.

The second door is private thermal and merchant power: Adani Power, JSW Energy, Tata Power, Torrent Power. Part of their output is sold under long contracts, part on the power exchange at whatever the day's price is. In a heatwave with plants short of coal, the exchange price can hit its cap and merchant plants mint money. In a cool, rainy summer, they sell at whatever they can get.

The third door is the renewable developer: Adani Green, NTPC Green, ACME Solar. They win auctions to sell solar or wind power at a fixed tariff for twenty-five years. No fuel bill, but a very big loan. Their return is basically the spread between that fixed tariff and the cost of money.

In power, the same heatwave is a windfall for one door, a footnote for another and an order book for a third.

The fourth door sells the shovels: Waaree and Premier Energies make solar modules and cells, Suzlon makes wind turbines, and IREDA lends to developers. Their fortunes ride the build-out pace and the import barriers that keep Chinese equipment out.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each from top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it explain how each gets paid: a regulated return, a mix of contracts and the exchange, a fixed twenty-five-year tariff, or a price per module, turbine or loan.
  • The tickers are the listed names behind each door. Click one to open its stock page. Tata Power and Torrent Power also own distribution networks, so they straddle more than one station in the next card.
  • The bar shows how much of the profit the company gets to keep. Here is the subtle part: the three generator doors all sit at medium. The bar does not separate them. What separates them is how steady that medium is. The regulated utility's slice is fixed by formula; the merchant plant's swings with the exchange price; the developer's is a thin, fixed spread over its cost of capital. Only the equipment door drops to low, because module makers compete with each other and with China on price.
  • The last line is the bet. Read them as four different macro views: capacity growth, demand outrunning supply, cheap capital, and the build-out pace.

The analogy underneath, the salaried government doctor, the private doctor in flu season, the clinic on a long lease and the equipment supplier, maps onto the tiles in order. Then apply the so-what: take any headline, a hot summer, a rate cut, a new duty on Chinese cells, and ask which tile it helps. Rarely is the answer all four.

c2.story:
The power kitchen starts in the ground, in the desert and in the river. Coal is dug by Coal India and captive mines, mostly in Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand, and hauled across the country by rail. NLC India digs lignite in Tamil Nadu. Coastal plants, like the ones at Mundra in Gujarat, burn imported coal instead. For renewables, the raw material is a site with strong sun or steady wind, and those cluster in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, usually far from the big cities.

Next comes equipment. BHEL builds the boilers and turbines for coal plants. For solar, the chain runs from polysilicon to wafers to cells to modules, and China dominates the first three links. Waaree and Premier assemble modules and increasingly make cells; Suzlon makes wind turbines. Batteries are overwhelmingly Chinese too.

At the third station, generation, the listed companies finally appear: NTPC, Adani Power, Adani Green, Tata Power, JSW Energy, NHPC and the rest. They build, finance and run the plants. Then the power leaves their hands. Power Grid's lines carry it across states, Grid-India balances the system second by second, and the exchanges trade the short-term slice.

Finally the state distribution companies, the discoms, buy most of the power and sell it to homes, farms and factories. And here is the weak link. Many discoms sell power below cost to farmers and households because state governments want them to, and they wait on subsidy cheques from those same governments. So they pay their own suppliers late.

A generator's real risk is rarely making the power. It is collecting the money for it.

That is why, for most of the last decade, the most important number on a generator's balance sheet was not capacity or plant load. It was how many months of revenue were stuck with discoms.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, from coal mine to customer, then the bands below.

The boxes are fuel and resource, equipment, generation, transmission and trading, and distribution. Under each, what happens and who stands there. Coal India and imported coal at the start; BHEL, Waaree, Premier and Suzlon next to Chinese suppliers at equipment; the listed generators in the middle; Power Grid, Grid-India and the exchanges in transmission; state discoms at the end.

The band row tells you who holds each station. Only one band, generation, carries the India listed colour. That is the striking part: the listed generators sit in a single box, buying fuel and equipment from others and selling to others. The equipment band is coloured as a rival: China upstream. The last band, state discoms, is the buyer for almost everything.

The second band row shows where the rival stands: China, for solar wafers, cells and batteries, repeated across the first four stations, with World at the last. Its grip is tightest at stations one and two, the raw inputs and the equipment, but it reaches into generation too, because a developer's biggest cost is the equipment China prices, and into the grid, as storage arrives with Chinese batteries. Indian module makers compete with it directly.

Two things the bands do not show. Tata Power and Torrent Power also run city distribution networks, so they reach into station five as well. And the equipment makers listed in door four of card one stand at station two, inside the band coloured as China's, which is exactly their competitive problem.

Use the diagram to trace headlines. A coal rake shortage starts at station one and hits thermal generators. A Chinese module price fall at station two cuts developers' capex and squeezes Indian makers. A state subsidy delay at station five travels all the way back as late payments to every generator.

c3.story:
Who actually buys Indian electricity? Almost everyone, but very few people write the cheque to a generator.

The customer of record is the state distribution company. It signs long power purchase agreements, often for twenty-five years, and buys most of the country's power. Its own customers are households, farmers, factories and shops, and its finances depend on its state government. If the state promises free power to farmers, as Punjab has for decades, the discom has to sell below cost and wait for a subsidy cheque. When the cheque is late, so are the generators' payments.

Households are the fastest-changing customers. Every new air conditioner adds to the summer evening peak, which is why heatwaves set new demand records almost every year in 2023 and 2024. Farmers draw power for irrigation pumps, so a weak monsoon means more pumping and more demand, and a strong one means less.

Then there is a newer, more interesting group of buyers who do not go through the discom at all. Large factories and exporters buy green power directly under open-access rules, because their foreign customers want low-carbon supply chains. Data centres, the cloud and AI build-out in Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad, want round-the-clock green power and sign private contracts for it. Railways and the green hydrogen mission want bulk renewable power.

And at the margin, there is the power exchange. When a heatwave hits, a hydro station runs dry or a coal plant trips, discoms rush to the exchange for short-term power, and prices spike. That is where merchant plants make their money.

The trend to watch is the slow shift from one buyer, the state discom, towards many private buyers with better credit. Each private contract is a little less discom risk in the system.
c3.read:
Seven tiles, one per customer group. Each reads in three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

The most useful way to read this grid is to sort the tiles by who writes the cheque.

  • The discom cheque: state distribution companies, households and farmers. Households and farmers create the demand, but the discom pays the generator. Look at what moves the discom tile: state finances, tariff revisions, subsidy payments. That is credit risk, not demand.
  • The private cheque: industry and commercial users, data centres, railways and green hydrogen. These buyers pay directly, usually with better credit, and they are the fastest-growing part of demand for renewable developers.
  • The spot cheque: power exchange buyers. This is the merchant plant's tile, and what moves it, heat waves, hydro output and plant outages, is pure weather and accident.

Now look at the third line of each tile again. Summer heat, monsoon, cloud and AI build-out, factory output: the demand drivers are a mix of weather and the economy. But the so-what line under the grid makes the key point: demand is set by weather and the economy, while the cheque is written by the discom, so its financial health is the industry's real credit risk.

Keep the data-centre tile in mind. It ties this industry to a global theme, and it explains why so many recent tenders ask for round-the-clock power rather than plain solar.

c4.story:
A coal plant is a taxi whose fuel bill the passenger pays. A solar park is a rickshaw with no fuel bill at all but a large loan on the vehicle. One cares about the price of coal; the other cares about the bank's interest rate. Hold that picture and the two profit and loss statements make sense.

For a regulated coal plant, fuel is the biggest cost by far, well over half of sales. But under regulated contracts most of that cost is passed through to the discom, so a coal price rise does not hurt the generator much. The merchant plant is a different animal: it bears the fuel cost itself, so imported coal prices and plant load decide whether it has a good or bad year. Plant load factor, how hard a plant actually runs compared with what it could, is the number that separates a merchant plant's fat year from a thin one.

The regulated utility's profit comes from the return on equity the regulator allows, a mid-teens percentage for central thermal plants. Change that norm and utility earnings move for years. Tax, by contrast, is largely passed through and barely matters.

Now the solar park. No fuel bill at all. Running costs are small: cleaning panels, maintenance, a few staff. What eats the revenue is depreciation and interest, because the developer borrowed most of the cost of the park. So a fall in interest rates is a direct gain in returns, and a rise is a direct loss.

A solar park is a bond with panels on top. The sunshine is free; the money is not.

Receivables used to be the silent killer for both. Discoms paid months late. The Late Payment Surcharge Rules of 2022 changed that, penalising late payers and letting generators cut supply to defaulters. Overdue dues dropped sharply, which is one reason the sector re-rated.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: one for a regulated thermal plant, one for a renewable developer. Read each left to right.

  • The input bar is fuel: coal, gas, lignite. On the thermal chart it takes well over half, close to three-fifths of sales. On the renewable chart it is empty. Zero. That blank space where the biggest bar should be is the whole renewable business model in one picture.
  • The opex bar is operations, maintenance and people, roughly a tenth on both charts.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is where the renewable chart fills up: close to three-fifths of sales goes to paying for the park and the loan. On the thermal chart it is around a seventh.
  • The last bar is what is left: about a sixth for thermal, about three-tenths for the renewable developer.

Look at the two charts together and you see the mirror image from the analogy: thermal spends its money on fuel, renewables spend theirs on capital. These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for amounts.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Fuel cost, depreciation, interest, capex, receivables and plant load factor all get a yes. Regulated return on equity gets a sometimes, because it matters enormously for door one and not at all for door three. Tax gets a no.

Then read the so-what as a checklist. For a coal name, read plant load factor and fuel pass-through. For a renewable name, read interest cost and commissioning pace.

c5.story:
Indian power has one of the longest and most painful cycles in the market, and many of the bankers who lived through the last one still flinch at the words coal plant.

The boom ran from 2007 to 2011. Demand forecasts were heroic, bank loans were easy, and private developers raced to build coal plants. The ultra mega power projects, Tata's at Mundra and Reliance Power's at Sasan, were the flagships. Then everything went wrong at once. Indonesia changed the rules on how its coal exports were priced, wrecking the economics of plants built on cheap imported coal. Domestic coal fell short. The coal-block allocation scandal broke, and in 2014 the Supreme Court cancelled almost all the coal blocks allotted since 1993. Discoms, broke, stopped signing contracts. Through to 2019, dozens of plants sat stranded, and banks booked some of the largest bad loans in their history.

The bottom came between 2019 and 2021. Stressed plants were sold cheaply to Adani Power, JSW Energy and others. Discom dues were restructured. And quietly, demand began to outrun supply. In October 2021 coal stocks at plants ran dangerously low. In 2022 record peak demand and coal shortages pushed exchange prices to their caps, and the railways cancelled passenger trains to run coal rakes. New late-payment rules forced discoms to clear old dues.

The boom was back. Heatwaves set records in 2023 and 2024. The government ordered new coal plants for the first time in years, and a wave of listings arrived: IREDA in 2023, then Premier Energies, Waaree, NTPC Green and ACME Solar in 2024, all at rich valuations. In late 2024, a US indictment of Adani executives shook the group's green arm.

Then 2025 was cool and rainy. Demand growth flattened, exchange prices fell, solar was curtailed at midday and module makers faced oversupply. That is where the clock stands: late in the boom, and cooling.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each come from the previous full cycle: the boom of 2007 to 2011, the peak in 2011 and 2012, the long bust from 2013 to 2019, and the bottom from 2019 to 2021. Notice how long that bust arc lasted: the better part of a decade. The arrow points into the middle of the peak arc, on the lower right, labelled late boom, cooling, with the detail capacity racing ahead of demand growth. The cycle has gone round once since the bottom; the new boom is not on the arcs but in the timeline beside it.

The timeline runs from 2019. Read the colours: 2019 is a bust year, 2020 and 2021 neutral, 2022 and the 2023 to 2024 entry both boom, 2025 neutral, and 2026 marked now. Two boom entries in a row followed by a neutral one is what a cycle rolling over looks like.

The four hands are what you watch to move the arrow.

  • Peak demand growth: moderate after a cool 2025, flat. A record-hot summer would revive the boom.
  • Exchange power prices: softer than the shortage years, pointing down. Merchant plants feel this first.
  • Signed contracts for auctioned renewables: backlog slowly clearing, mixed.
  • Module and cell prices: falling on oversupply, pointing down. Good for developers, bad for makers.

No hand points firmly up. That is why the so-what says regulated utilities hold up best late in a capacity boom, while merchant plants and equipment makers feel the glut first.

c6.story:
A power company's year is decided by a weather forecaster, a central banker and a coal railway dispatcher, roughly in that order.

The first three-dot dial is electricity demand, and in India that largely means heat. A scorching summer drives the evening peak, fills thermal plants and sends exchange prices up. A cool, rainy one, like 2025, does the opposite. This dial matters most to merchant plants and private thermal names, and the India Meteorological Department's summer forecast is effectively an earnings preview for them.

The second three-dot dial is interest rates. A renewable developer's biggest cost is the loan on its parks, so when the Reserve Bank cuts rates and bond yields fall, every project's return improves and the stocks re-rate. When rates rise, the opposite. If demand is the thermal dial, rates are the renewable dial.

Then the two-dot dials. Domestic coal output decides whether thermal plants run smoothly or scramble for expensive imports. Imported coal prices squeeze merchant and coastal plants, though contracted plants pass them through. Chinese module and cell prices cut both ways: cheaper panels lower developers' capex but squeeze Indian makers like Waaree and Premier. Discom finances decide how fast generators are paid and whether new contracts get signed. Industrial output adds baseload demand.

And the one-dot dials. The monsoon fills hydro reservoirs and cuts farm pumping, which helps hydro and hurts thermal. The rupee raises the cost of imported coal, equipment and dollar bonds. And a final dial, energy-sector sentiment, is a reminder that listed power names often trade as a basket: when the theme is in favour, everything rises together, and when it falls out, the regulated utilities get sold with the module makers, whatever their fundamentals.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial. Read across: the dial, the channel it travels through, what a rise does, and its weight in dots.

  • The arrow: green up means a rise helps the industry, red down means it hurts, a diamond means it depends. Chinese module prices and the monsoon carry diamonds, because each helps one door and hurts another.
  • The weight: three dots for demand and interest rates. Everything else is two or one.

Today's reading column fills where a dial maps to a series we track. Electricity demand maps to the core-sector electricity index, interest rates to the money-market rate, domestic coal to the core-sector coal index, industrial output to the electricity component of industrial production, the rupee to the dollar rate, and sentiment to the Nifty Energy index. Imported coal, Chinese module prices, discom finances and the monsoon show a dash; for those you follow the news and company commentary.

Now pair the three-dot rows with the doors. Demand points at doors two and one: merchant and thermal. Interest rates point at door three: developers. That pairing is why the so-what says that if you track only two dials, track peak demand and rates.

Finally, scan the arrows for today's situation. Demand is soft after 2025, which hurts the demand-led doors, while rates were cut through 2025, which helps the rate-led door. The dials themselves explain why the call prefers developers with signed contracts over merchant coal plants right now.

c7.story:
India wants to build a staggering amount of power capacity, coal for the evening peak and solar, wind and storage for everything else. The bottleneck table explains why the build-out happens in fits and starts.

The first is structural and old: discom finances. Distribution companies lose money on subsidised farm and household power, so they pay late and hesitate to sign new contracts. The 2022 late-payment rules helped a great deal, but they treat the symptom. The cause, selling below cost for political reasons, is still there.

The second is new and also structural, and it comes from physics rather than politics. Solar floods the grid at noon and vanishes at sunset. Midday prices on the exchange collapse, and then, just as households come home and switch on their air conditioners, there is an evening shortage that only coal, hydro or batteries can fill. Grid engineers call the shape of net demand through the day the duck curve.

India does not have a shortage of power. It has a shortage of power at seven in the evening.

You can see the consequence everywhere: tenders asking for round-the-clock or storage-backed power, a fresh wave of coal plants for the evening peak, and pumped storage, using cheap noon power to pump water uphill for release after dark.

The recurring bottlenecks are about wires and wagons. Desert solar parks are built faster than the lines that carry their power, so finished plants wait or are curtailed. In a heatwave, coal rakes run short and plants run low on fuel, as in 2022. The Chinese supply chain cuts both ways: duties protect Indian makers but raise developers' costs. Land and forest clearances slow hydro and thermal. And the unsigned auction backlog, capacity auctioned by central agencies that discoms have not agreed to buy, leaves projects waiting for a customer.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity tag. The tag tells you where each risk belongs.

  • Structural: discom finances and solar's midday glut. Two permanent features, one financial and one physical. The first caps returns across the industry; the second decides which kind of capacity earns the best price from here on, which is storage and evening power, not plain solar.
  • Recurring: transmission lagging generation, and coal logistics. These come back every year, usually in summer, and move individual stocks for a quarter.
  • Two-sided: the Chinese supply chain. The duties and made-in-India lists that protect Waaree and Premier are the same ones that raise Adani Green's and NTPC Green's costs. Which side you are on depends on the door.
  • Slow: land and approvals. They delay projects, mostly hydro and thermal, by years, but rarely surprise.
  • Cyclical: the unsigned auction backlog. It builds up in a boom, when auctions run ahead of discom demand, and clears as demand catches up.

Read the so-what line with the table in view: discom finances and transmission set the speed limit on the build-out; the midday glut decides which kind of capacity earns the best price next. If you own a developer, ask two questions from this table at every results call: how much of its pipeline has a signed contract, and how much has a transmission connection?

c8.story:
In power, the rulebook is not background noise. It writes the income statement.

For the regulated utilities, the most important document is the central regulator's tariff order. CERC sets the return on equity central plants may earn, and that norm is the profit engine for NTPC and NHPC for years at a time. CERC also regulates the power exchanges and, in the shortage of 2022, capped their prices. State regulators approve discom tariffs and power purchases, which decides whether discoms can afford new contracts.

The rule that changed the industry's credit quality is the Late Payment Surcharge Rules of 2022. Before them, discoms routinely sat on generators' bills for months. The rules penalised late payment and let generators stop supplying defaulters. Old dues were cleared in instalments, and receivable days fell sharply. If you want one reason the sector re-rated after 2022, this is a good candidate.

For renewables, demand is partly created by rule. Renewable purchase and consumption obligations require discoms and large users to buy a rising share of green power. For equipment makers, protection is created by rule too. Basic customs duty on Chinese modules and cells began in 2022. The approved list of models and manufacturers, ALMM, restricts government-linked projects to approved, mostly Indian-made modules, and from June 2026 the rule extends to cells. That is a gift to integrated makers who produce their own cells and a squeeze on assemblers who import them.

On the thermal side, the Ministry of Power has directed new coal capacity to meet the evening peak, a sharp turn from the years when nobody would finance a coal plant. Two rules are coming: India's carbon credit trading scheme, which would add a cost to coal and revenue to green power, and American trade action on Indian solar exports, which threatens module makers' export orders.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule: what it does, why you care, and its status.

  • Always: CERC and the state regulators. These set returns and approve purchases. They rarely make headlines, but a change to the return norm moves regulated earnings for years.
  • Live: the late-payment rules, customs duty and anti-dumping on solar imports, renewable purchase obligations, and the ministry's push for new coal capacity. Four live rows, and they point in different directions: two help generators get paid and sell, one protects makers, one revives thermal.
  • New: the ALMM lists, with cells added from June 2026. This is the most consequential new rule for door four.
  • Coming: the carbon credit trading scheme and US trade action on Indian solar exports.

Now map rows to doors, because each door lives under a different part of the table. Regulated utilities live under CERC. Private thermal names live under the late-payment rules and the new-coal directive. Renewable developers live under purchase obligations, and pay for the ALMM and customs rows through higher equipment costs. Equipment makers live under ALMM and customs duty for protection, and under the US trade row for risk.

Notice the tension that creates: the same row, ALMM, is a tailwind for Waaree and Premier and a headwind for developers. When you read regulatory news for this industry, always ask which door is on which side of it.

Dated regulatory news filtered for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces ask who gets to keep the money. In power, the answer depends almost entirely on whether a regulator is standing between you and the market.

The regulated utility barely faces competition. Its plants are not bidding against anyone each day; the regulator sets a tariff that covers costs and a return on equity. New entrants are not a worry either: a large coal or hydro plant takes years, land, clearances and thousands of crores, and newcomers almost never try. Its main pressure is the buyer, the discoms, who are few, state-owned and slow to pay. The late-payment rules shifted some power back to generators, but the buyer spoke still carries weight.

The renewable developer lives on the other side of the fence. Solar is easy to enter: buy land, buy modules, connect to the grid. So auctions are cut-throat reverse auctions, where the lowest tariff wins, and tariffs have been driven down to remarkably thin spreads over the cost of capital. The merchant plant competes on price every single day on the exchange. Both depend on suppliers they do not control: Chinese equipment for developers, Coal India and lenders for everyone.

Regulation is a cage and a shield. The regulated utility cannot earn more than its allowed return, but nobody can make it earn much less.

Substitutes are a slow, real threat for both. Rooftop solar, pushed by the PM Surya Ghar scheme launched in 2024, and captive green power for large factories let the biggest and best-paying users bypass the discom. That does not hurt the generator directly, but it takes the discom's best customers, which weakens the payer every generator depends on.

The so-what sums it up: regulated utilities keep a steady, guaranteed slice; developers keep a thin spread; merchant plants keep a lot in a shortage and little in a glut.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes: rivalry at the top, then clockwise supplier power, buyer power, new entrants and substitutes. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force applies. Smaller shape, better business.

Two shapes are drawn: regulated utilities, and renewable developers with merchant plants. The size difference is dramatic. The regulated shape is small and pinched: just half a point on rivalry and on entrants, the two spokes at the top and lower left, so it barely leaves the centre there. It bulges only on buyer power, at two, and a little on supplier power at one and a half.

The developer and merchant shape is large and fairly round: two and a half on rivalry, two on supplier power, two and a half on buyer power, two on entrants. It is the shape of an open, competitive market, which is exactly what renewable auctions and the exchange are.

Now find where the shapes come closest. It is on buyer power and substitutes. Both doors sell mainly to discoms, so both carry buyer pressure, and both face the slow drift of large users to rooftop and captive power. The big gaps are on rivalry and entrants, the two forces the regulator removes.

The table beside the chart gives each score with a one-line reason. Use it to adjust the shapes for a specific company: a developer with mostly private, round-the-clock contracts with data centres would pull in its buyer spoke, while a merchant plant selling largely on the exchange would push rivalry to the edge.

c10.story:
A power company's results deck can run to dozens of slides of maps, capacity charts and project timelines. Eight numbers tell you almost everything, as long as you remember which door you are looking at.

Start with plant load factor for thermal names, how hard the coal plants actually ran. In a shortage it climbs high; in a glut it sags, and merchant earnings sag with it. Then capacity added and under construction, because for regulated utilities and developers the future is literally the capital work in progress, plants being built that will earn once they are commissioned. Commissioning on schedule matters more than the size of the pipeline.

Next, EBITDA margin, which mostly tells you the business mix. Renewables run very high margins because they have no fuel bill; regulated thermal runs far lower because fuel is a pass-through that inflates sales without adding profit. A thermal name whose margin jumps is often selling more on the exchange.

Then the money questions. Receivable days tell you how fast discoms are paying; after the 2022 rules, this should be low and stable. Net debt to EBITDA tells you whether a developer can fund its pipeline. Interest as a share of EBITDA tells you how much of the operating profit the lenders take, which, for a developer, is the number that rate cuts improve.

Power and fuel cost share shows fuel exposure. A stable share with pass-through is healthy; a spike hurts merchant plants that bear their own fuel. Finally, return on capital employed tells you whether all that building earns its keep, a question that matters a lot when capacity is racing ahead of demand, as the clock says it is now.
c10.read:
One row per number: what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from listed companies' latest annual filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask. Several rows are door-specific: plant load factor and fuel share for thermal, interest share and debt for developers.
  • What good looks like gives the rules of thumb: plant load above three-quarters for coal, with anything above four-fifths signalling a shortage; EBITDA margins above four-fifths for renewables and in the mid to high twenties for regulated thermal; receivables under two months; debt under five times EBITDA for renewables and under three for thermal; interest taking less than about a third of EBITDA; return on capital in the low teens. Benchmarks, not targets.
  • Today's industry median is the typical listed company's figure.

Only the plant load factor row shows a dash, because it comes from company disclosures and grid data, not filings. Every other row has a median, which makes this one of the better-covered cheat sheets on the page.

Read the medians with one caution: they blend four doors. A median EBITDA margin sits somewhere between a solar developer and a coal utility and describes neither. The more useful medians here are receivable days, which tell you whether the late-payment rules are still holding across the industry, and interest as a share of EBITDA, which tells you how much the sector as a whole stands to gain from rate cuts.

For any one company, compare its number with the good mark for its own door, then glance at the median to see where it sits in the pack.

c11.story:
Power is an industry where the weather forecast is a stock tip, and the outside signals arrive at three different speeds.

The fastest are same-quarter signals. Exchange prices move merchant revenue with each day's trading; a week of high prices in May is visible in that quarter's results. Coal stocks at power plants are published regularly; when they run low, generation is lost and plants buy expensive imported coal in the same quarter.

The one-quarter signals are the forecaster's toolkit. The India Meteorological Department's summer and monsoon outlook tells you about peak demand and hydro output a quarter ahead. The repo rate and bond yields reset developers' funding costs within a quarter. Chinese polysilicon and module prices flow into Indian makers' prices and developers' capex. Discom dues data warns of receivable stress. And industrial output growth turns into baseload power demand.

The slowest signal is the most strategic: power purchase agreements signed from central auctions. A contract signed today becomes a commissioned, earning project around two quarters later. When signing slows, the developers' growth slows after it.

Now the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when peak demand grows faster than capacity, exchange prices are firm, and interest rates are falling. Today only one of the three signs is on. Demand did not outgrow capacity after a cool 2025, and exchange prices are softer than in the shortage years. Interest rates, though, were cut through 2025. One of three means a glut is forming.

That is why the call prefers regulated utilities, whose returns do not depend on exchange prices, and developers with signed contracts and storage, who benefit from the one sign still on, over merchant coal plants and module makers who are exposed to the glut.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel it travels through.

Read it in three groups.

  • Same quarter, left: exchange prices and coal stocks at plants. These are real-time; they tell you what this quarter already looks like.
  • One quarter ahead, middle: the weather forecast, rates and yields, Chinese module prices, discom dues and industrial output. This crowded middle is your main reading list.
  • Two quarters ahead, right: signed power purchase agreements. A lone dot, but the one that best predicts developers' growth.

Below the chart, the rule shows three signs. Demand outgrowing capacity has a cross, noted cool 2025, steady not surging. Exchange prices firm has a cross, softer than the shortage years. Interest rates falling has a tick, rate cuts through 2025. One tick of three is the rule's warning reading: a glut forming. Compare that with the clock in card five, where the arrow sits in the peak arc. The two cards agree.

Then the call box gives the headline, three points, and what would change the call: a record-hot summer pushing demand and exchange prices back to shortage levels, a rise in interest rates, or a deterioration in discom finances. Notice each of those maps to one of the dots: the weather forecast, the repo rate, the discom dues data. Watch those three dots and you will know when to revisit the call.
